query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The early onset of corrosion-related degradation in pre-exposure Q235 steel is driven by non-uniform formation of its naturally developing passive iron oxide film. In regions with higher defect density (such as grain boundaries, inclusions, or residual stresses), the passive film is thinner or chemically inhomogeneous. Under harsh environments containing aggressive ions (like Cl–) and at elevated temperatures, these localized weak spots promote differential aeration and the initiation of pitting corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its unmodified, pre-exposure state with its inherent microstructural heterogeneities (grain boundaries, inclusions, and residual stresses) and a naturally forming, but unoptimized, iron oxide film.
generation.intervention: Prepare batches of Q235 steel samples that are intentionally modified to have either a minimized surface defect density (via electropolishing and appropriate annealing) or an increased defect density (via controlled mechanical deformation). Expose these samples to a defined aggressive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) at both room temperature and a selected elevated temperature (e.g., ~70°C).
generation.conditions: Testing in a corrosive aqueous environment containing chloride ions, under well-controlled oxygenation levels. Comparisons will be made at room temperature and at an elevated temperature representative of harsh service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local variations in the density of microstructural defects (grain boundaries, inclusions) and the resulting non-uniformity in the protective oxide film (passive layer) that forms naturally on Q235 steel.
generation.mechanism: At defect-free regions, a uniform and protective iron oxide layer forms that retards further corrosion. However, at mechanically or microstructurally defective sites, the oxide film is either thinner or disrupted, creating local anodic sites. In the presence of chloride ions—with their high ability to penetrate oxide films—and under elevated temperature (which accelerates ion mobility and film breakdown), these areas become preferential sites for pit initiation and subsequent corrosion propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with a higher density of surface defects (or artificially enhanced heterogeneity) should exhibit earlier onset and more severe pitting corrosion (higher local corrosion rates, lower passivation potentials) than those with minimized defects. In both types, elevated temperature conditions will lead to more rapid breakdown of the passive layer and increased corrosion severity compared to room temperature, when compared to untreated/reference samples.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples with the standard as-received surface finish and typical microstructural heterogeneities, expected to form a relatively uniform passive film in benign conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply to Q235 steel exposed to chloride-containing environments under moderate oxygen levels. The observed effects and their magnitudes may vary with differences in specific microstructural features and environmental conditions; the mechanism may differ if protective coatings or alloying modifications are present.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of various defect types (grain boundaries versus non-metallic inclusions) to passive film breakdown, and the precise influence of temperature on passive film degradation kinetics in Q235 steel, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set with minimized surface defects (by means of electropolishing followed by annealing) and one set with intentionally increased defect density (by controlled mechanical deformation). Expose both sets to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under identical conditions at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (around 70°C). Monitor the evolution of the passive film and the onset of corrosion using electrochemical techniques and surface microscopy.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization testing to determine corrosion potentials and current densities
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess passive film integrity
Surface analyses (optical and electron microscopy) to evaluate pitting density and morphology over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences in the timing or severity of pitting corrosion (as indicated by similar corrosion current densities, passivation behaviors, and pit densities) are observed between the low-defect and high-defect samples—both at room temperature and at elevated temperature—then the hypothesis that localized microstructural defects mediate passive film breakdown and subsequent corrosion in Q235 steel would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.
